newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi upbeat on economy, Europe.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi upbeat on economy, Europe.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Friday that his first six months in office had brought Italy within reach of entering Europe's planned single currency and had improved its economic performance beyond expectations.
"I have based the government's entire policy on entering Europe," Prodi told an end-of-year news conference.
"In May, financial analysts gave us a 10 percent chance. Now it's 60 percent. It's not 100 percent, but it's not bad."
Prodi, who took office in May at the head of a centre-left government, has said Italy must not fail to be among the founder members of Economic and Monetary Union when it starts in 1999.

But he said his efforts, which have included an austerity 1997 budget to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off Italy's bulging debts, would have been needed in any case "to get Italy out of a crisis that has lasted for 30 years".
The appointment with Europe had just speeded efforts up, he said, but congratulated himself on progress to date.
"The economy is recovering much better than forecast. Despite talk of falling consumption, I look at the figures every day and they are not falling," he said.
Six months ago, Italy failed to make the grade on any of the five criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty as goals to be reached by 1998 to qualify for EMU, Prodi said.
But now Italy had lowered inflation to 2.6 percent, nearly two percentage points lower than in May, slashed interest rates to 7.5 percent and rejoined Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism.
On the key target -- reducing the annual deficit to three percent of Gross Domestic Product -- Prodi admitted there was still work to do. "We're not yet there, but we're very close."

He gave no figures. Officially, the government maintains it will reach the target in time, and Prodi said he was not worried by the fifth Maastricht goal, that of reducing total debts, because he thought very few states would manage to meet it.
Many economic analysts and the opposition believe that Prodi's Herculean efforts will still not be enough to qualify Italy for EMU, leaving him no option but to pass a mini-budget.

Prodi, who says interest rate developments could change the scenario, would not be drawn on whether another set of measures was necessary. He said the government would decide at the end of February or early March when 1996 accounts were published.
"If a mini-budget is needed, it will be very limited," he said, adding that it would come "totally through spending cuts".
The 1997 budget, which is nearing final parliamentary approval, has been criticised for being over-heavy on tax, including a one-off "Euro-tax" levy to raise 12.5 trillion lire.
But Prodi ducked criticism, saying he had no option but to dispense bitter medicine, and launched straight into a row with union leaders over a review of Italy's generous pensions system.
Prodi said Italy had to raise the limit for qualifying for a pension and told trades union leaders they must not refuse to begin discussions on the pension system next year.
A review of a 1995 pension reform deal, which economists say is badly needed, is due to be carried out in 1998 but Prodi wants to bring it forward by a year. Unions refuse point blank.

"It is not possible to delay the discussions," Prodi said. "I do not intend to smash the pension system but to bring about the necessary reforms so that the cash to pay pensions is really there and pensions are not paid out of an accumulation of debt."
